mcqs.question: An analytical query selects 2 columns out of 40 across 100 million rows. Why does a column-oriented format serve this faster than a row-oriented one?
options: It reads only the bytes for the 2 needed columns instead of pulling every field of every row along with them
Column-oriented formats compress better regardless of query shape
Row-oriented formats cannot be queried by SQL engines at all
Column-oriented formats always store fewer total rows than row-oriented ones
mcqs.explanation: Because column orientation lays each field out contiguously, the engine can skip the 38 unneeded columns entirely, while a row-oriented format has to read every field of every row just to extract the 2 it wants. Row-oriented formats are fully queryable by SQL engines; the difference is efficiency, not capability, and row count is unrelated to orientation.

mcqs.question: You're designing a high-throughput event pipeline where producers write one full event at a time and need safe schema evolution. Which format fits best?
options: Parquet, because it's the most widely supported analytical format
CSV, because it has the lowest per-record overhead
Avro, because it's row-oriented for whole-record writes and carries an evolvable schema
ORC, because it's optimized for Hive-based batch scans
mcqs.explanation: Avro's row orientation matches writing and reading whole records one at a time, and its schema evolution support is built for exactly this kind of streaming producer/consumer setup. Parquet and ORC are columnar and want data batched in large groups to compress well, making them a poor fit for single-record streaming writes, and CSV carries no schema at all.

mcqs.question: A 50GB gzip-compressed CSV file is loaded into a 10-worker Spark cluster, but the job runs on effectively one worker. Why?
options: Spark cannot read CSV files under any circumstances
CSV files require a schema to be split across workers
The file is too large for Spark to load into memory at all
Gzip compression isn't splittable, so decompression must proceed sequentially from the start of the file, preventing parallel chunking
mcqs.explanation: Gzip's compression format requires sequential decoding from the beginning, so a single gzip file can't be divided into independent chunks for parallel workers — one worker ends up doing all the decompression. Spark reads CSV fine, doesn't need to fit the whole file in memory to process it, and the missing-schema issue is a separate problem from splittability.

mcqs.question: A team picks JSON for a 500GB analytical dataset because it's "easy to read." What's the main cost of that choice at that scale?
options: JSON files cannot be loaded into any warehouse or query engine
JSON cannot represent numeric data types, only strings
Row-oriented, verbose text forces the engine to parse and discard unneeded columns per record, making queries far slower and more expensive than a columnar format
The cost is purely aesthetic — query performance is unaffected by file format
mcqs.explanation: JSON's row-oriented, text-heavy structure means every query pays to parse and discard unneeded fields per record, which compounds badly at hundreds of gigabytes compared to a columnar format that skips unneeded columns entirely. JSON does support numeric types and loads into most engines fine — the real cost is in query performance and compute spend, not capability.

mcqs.question: Why would writing Parquet files one record at a time, instead of in large batches, be a bad idea?
options: Parquet files cannot be written by streaming systems under any configuration
Columnar formats need many rows batched together to compress and organize well; single-record writes produce poor compression and many small files
Parquet has no concept of a schema, so single-record writes lose type information
Writing Parquet one record at a time is functionally identical to writing Avro one record at a time
mcqs.explanation: Columnar formats get their compression and scan efficiency from grouping many rows together per column; writing one record at a time defeats that and creates a small-file overhead problem instead. Parquet does carry a schema, and it behaves quite differently from Avro under single-record writes precisely because of orientation.

mcqs.question: A source system exports data as CSV by default because that's its easiest export option. What's the recommended approach for a pipeline feeding an analytical warehouse?
options: Convert to a columnar, schema-carrying format like Parquet during ingestion, before the data lands for analytical use
Keep CSV as the resting format throughout the pipeline since it's simplest to maintain
Only convert format if the dataset exceeds 1TB
Switch the source system to export Avro instead of CSV
mcqs.explanation: Converting to Parquet during ingestion captures the performance and schema benefits for every downstream analytical query, and this conversion is cheap relative to living with a poor resting format for years. Waiting for a size threshold means paying the cost at every smaller scale too, and rewriting the source system is usually not something a data engineer controls or should attempt just for format reasons.
